title: Personal Identity: What Makes You You?
subtitle: Memories, bodies, teleporters and the question of what really matters
objectives: By the end you will be able to distinguish numerical from qualitative identity and explain the persistence question.
By the end you will be able to reconstruct Locke's memory theory and the objections of Reid and Butler, and explain how psychological continuity theories answer them.
By the end you will be able to analyze the ship of Theseus, teletransportation and fission cases.
By the end you will be able to explain Parfit's claim that identity is not what matters, and compare it with animalism and narrative views.
hook:
Look at a photograph of yourself at age five. Almost every atom in that child's body has since been replaced. The child's beliefs, tastes, fears and plans are unrecognizable. You remember little or nothing of the day the photograph was taken. Yet you say, without hesitation, "That's me." What makes it true?

The question is not idle. It shapes whether you should fear your own death, whether you can be punished for a crime you committed decades ago, whether a person with advanced dementia is bound by wishes they expressed when well, and whether stepping into a teleporter would be a trip or a suicide. On Day 47 you met Locke's empiricism, and on Day 50 Hume's view that the self is only a bundle of perceptions. This lesson returns to Locke's own theory of personal identity, the starting point of a debate that, after Derek Parfit, ended with one of the most surprising conclusions in modern philosophy: that personal identity may not be what matters.

sections.heading: Identity, Sameness and the Persistence Question
sections.body:
First, clear away an ambiguity. "Identical" has two senses.
- **Qualitative identity** is exact similarity. Two new coins from the same mint are qualitatively identical: they share all their properties.
- **Numerical identity** is being one and the same thing. The coin in your pocket today is numerically identical to the coin you received yesterday, even though it has been scratched since.

The puzzle of personal identity concerns numerical identity over time, despite qualitative change. This is the **persistence question**: under what conditions is a person existing at one time the same person as a person existing at another time?

An old puzzle shows how hard persistence questions are, even for objects. The Greek biographer Plutarch (c. 46–120 CE) reported that the Athenians preserved the ship of the hero Theseus, replacing rotting planks with new timber over the years, until philosophers debated whether it was still the same ship. Thomas Hobbes, in *De Corpore* (1655), added a twist. Suppose someone kept every discarded plank and reassembled them into a ship. Now there are two candidates: the continuously repaired ship and the reassembled one. Which is the ship of Theseus?

The **ship of Theseus** shows that our criteria for identity can pull in different directions, here **spatiotemporal continuity** (the repaired ship) versus **sameness of parts** (the reassembled one). Many philosophers think there is no deep fact here: "same ship" is a concept with criteria that usually coincide, and in strange cases we must simply decide what to say. The question is whether persons are like that too. It seems that, for persons, there *must* be a deep fact. If I am about to be tortured, it matters enormously whether the person who will suffer is me.

sections.heading: Locke's Memory Theory and Its Critics
sections.body:
John Locke added a chapter, "Of Identity and Diversity," to the second edition of his *Essay Concerning Human Understanding* (1694). It set the agenda for three centuries.

Locke distinguished three things: the same **substance** (material or immaterial), the same **man** (the same living human organism) and the same **person**. A person, he wrote, is "a thinking intelligent being, that has reason and reflection, and can consider itself as itself, the same thinking thing, in different times and places." What makes a person the same over time is **consciousness**: as far as consciousness can be extended backward to any past action or thought, so far reaches the identity of that person. In practice, this has usually been read as a **memory criterion**: you are the same person as someone in the past if you can remember, from the inside, that person's experiences or actions.

Locke illustrated his view with a thought experiment. Suppose the soul of a prince, carrying with it the consciousness of the prince's past life, entered the body of a cobbler. The resulting being would be the same *man* as the cobbler, but, Locke said, everyone would see he was the same *person* as the prince. Personhood follows consciousness, not body. Locke also emphasized that "person" is a **forensic** term, a term of law and morality: it concerns who can be held responsible, punished and rewarded, and who has a stake in their future.

Two classic objections followed.

**Reid's brave officer.** Thomas Reid (1785) imagined a boy flogged for robbing an orchard, who later, as a young officer, captures an enemy standard in battle, and who later still becomes a general. The officer remembers the flogging; the general remembers capturing the standard but has forgotten the flogging. On the memory criterion, the officer is the boy, and the general is the officer, but the general is not the boy. Yet identity is **transitive**: if A is B and B is C, then A must be C. The memory theory contradicts itself.

**Butler's circularity.** Joseph Butler (1736) objected that memory presupposes identity rather than constituting it. A real memory of doing something is a memory of something *I* did. So we cannot define personal identity in terms of memory without assuming personal identity already. Merely seeming to remember storming the Bastille does not make you a revolutionary of 1789.

sections.heading: Psychological Continuity and Its Rival, Animalism
sections.body:
Twentieth-century philosophers repaired Locke's theory to meet these objections.

To answer Reid, they distinguished direct **psychological connections** (such as a memory of a particular experience, or an intention carried out later) from **psychological continuity**, which is an overlapping chain of such connections. The general is directly connected to the officer and the officer to the boy, so the general is psychologically continuous with the boy, like a rope whose individual fibers never run its whole length. Continuity, unlike direct memory, is transitive. The theory was also broadened beyond memory to include the persistence of beliefs, desires, intentions and character.

To answer Butler, Sydney Shoemaker (1970) introduced **quasi-memory**: a state just like a memory, caused in the right way by a past experience, but without the built-in assumption that the experience was one's own. If quasi-memories are possible, then the **psychological continuity theory** can define personal identity without circularity: you are the same person as a past person if you are psychologically continuous with them, through the right kind of causal chain.

This view is probably the most widely held, but it has a powerful rival. **Animalism**, defended by Eric Olson (*The Human Animal*, 1997) and Paul Snowdon, says that each of us is a human animal, a biological organism, and that our persistence conditions are biological: we persist as long as the organism stays alive. Animalism's chief argument is the **too many thinkers problem**. There is a human animal sitting in your chair, thinking your thoughts. If you are a person in Locke's sense and not that animal, then there are two thinkers in your chair, and you cannot know which one you are. Simpler to say you *are* the animal.

Animalism's cost is that it rejects the prince and the cobbler. If your brain, with all your memories and character, were transplanted into another body, animalism suggests you would not go with it (though some animalists argue a living brain is a sort of maximally mutilated animal). It also implies that you were once a fetus with no psychology at all, and might continue to exist in a persistent vegetative state. Some find these implications correct; others find them absurd.

sections.heading: Teletransporters, Branch Lines and Fission
sections.body:
Derek Parfit's *Reasons and Persons* (1984) used thought experiments drawn from science fiction to test these theories.

**Teletransportation.** You enter a booth on Earth. A scanner records the exact state of every cell in your body and brain, destroying them in the process. The information is sent to Mars, where a replicator builds an exact copy from new matter. The person who steps out on Mars has your memories, character and plans, and believes he has just traveled. Have you traveled, or have you died and been replaced by a copy? The psychological continuity theory (if it allows any reliable cause) says you have traveled. A physical or animalist view says you have died.

**The Branch Line case.** Now suppose the scanner malfunctions and does not destroy your body. The replica on Mars is created, but you remain on Earth, and you are told that the scanner has damaged your heart and you will die within days. The replica, on Mars, will carry on your life. It now seems clear that *you* are the one on Earth who will die, and that the replica is someone else. But the replica's relation to you is exactly the same as it was in the ordinary case. Doesn't that show that in the ordinary case, too, the replica is someone else?

**Fission.** The deepest case does not even require science fiction teleporters. Patients whose brain hemispheres have been surgically separated show that each hemisphere can support a stream of consciousness. Imagine (following David Wiggins, 1967, and Parfit, 1971) that your brain is divided and each half is transplanted into a different body, and that each resulting person is psychologically continuous with you. Call them Lefty and Righty. What happened to you? There are only a few options:
1. You died. But this is strange: if only one half had been transplanted successfully, we would say you survived. How can a double success be a failure?
2. You are Lefty, not Righty (or vice versa). But they are perfectly symmetrical; nothing could make it one rather than the other.
3. You are both. But Lefty and Righty soon lead different lives, with different experiences and beliefs; they are clearly two people, and one person cannot be two.

Since identity must be one-one, and the relation you bear to each is one-many, none of the options is satisfactory. Parfit concluded that the question "Am I Lefty or Righty?" may have no answer, and that we should stop asking it.

sections.heading: Parfit: Identity Is Not What Matters
sections.body:
Parfit's conclusion was radical. In fission, you do not survive as Lefty or Righty, if survival requires identity. But consider what you get: two people who each remember your life, continue your projects and love your friends. Ordinary death would give you none of this. So, Parfit argued, fission is about as good as ordinary survival. If that is right, what we care about in caring about survival cannot be identity itself. It must be something that can hold in a one-many form: what Parfit called **Relation R**, psychological connectedness and continuity, with any cause.

This is the thesis that **identity is not what matters**. Usually, Relation R and identity go together, so we do not notice the difference. But when they come apart, R is what we should care about. Personal identity is then like the identity of a nation or a club: a matter of degree in hard cases, and not a further deep fact. Parfit called his view **reductionism**: the existence of a person just consists in the existence of a body and brain and a series of interrelated physical and mental events.

Parfit described the personal effect of accepting this view. He had, he said, seemed to live in a glass tunnel, at the end of which was darkness. When he changed his view, "the walls of my glass tunnel disappeared." He cared less about his own death, and more about the lives of others, because the boundary between his future and theirs no longer seemed so deep. He noted the resemblance to the Buddha's teaching of no-self (*anattā*), and to Hume's bundle view (Day 50).

The view has implications for ethics. If personal identity is a matter of degree, perhaps my relation to my distant future self is less close than my relation to my tomorrow self, which might justify some forms of discounting the future, or might mean that a long-ago criminal deserves less punishment if they have greatly changed. It also supports impartial moral theories like the ones in the Ethics track: if the boundaries between persons are less deep, the boundaries' moral importance may be less too.

Critics have pushed back. Bernard Williams's paper "The Self and the Future" (1970) showed that our intuitions shift with framing: told that "you" will be tortured after your memories are swapped into another body, you fear for yourself, though psychological continuity says you will escape. Mark Johnston and others argued that the strangeness of fission does not show what matters in ordinary life. And narrative theorists, such as Marya Schechtman (*The Constitution of Selves*, 1996), argue that what makes a life one person's is not a bare chain of connections but a self-told story that integrates experiences into a meaningful whole, which gives identity a richer role than Parfit allows.

keyQuote.text: A thinking intelligent being, that has reason and reflection, and can consider itself as itself, the same thinking thing, in different times and places.
keyQuote.source: John Locke, An Essay Concerning Human Understanding (2nd edition, 1694), Book II, chapter 27, defining a person

modernConnection.title: Dementia, Advance Directives and the Two Selves
modernConnection.body:
In a 1991 article in the *Journal of the American Medical Association*, a medical student named Andrew Firlik described Margo, a woman with Alzheimer's disease who seemed, as far as anyone could tell, very happy: she painted the same picture every day, reread the same pages of a book, and enjoyed peanut butter and jelly sandwiches. The case was later made famous by the legal philosopher Ronald Dworkin, who posed a hard question. Suppose that, years earlier, when she was well, Margo had signed an advance directive saying that if she developed dementia, she should not be treated for any other life-threatening illness. Now she develops pneumonia, while apparently content. Should the doctors follow the directive?

Dworkin, in *Life's Dominion* (1993), argued yes: the earlier Margo's **precedent autonomy** should govern, because her considered values about the shape of her whole life deserve respect. The legal scholar Rebecca Dresser replied that the current Margo's interests, in a life she seems to enjoy, should take priority, especially if the earlier and later Margo are psychologically so different that the earlier one's wishes look more like those of a different person.

This is the theory of personal identity in a hospital ward. On the psychological continuity view, advanced dementia may weaken Relation R so much that the person who signed the directive and the person now in the bed are only loosely connected, which might strengthen Dresser's case. Animalism says the same human being persists throughout, which may support Dworkin's view that one person's earlier choices bind her later life. A narrative theorist might ask which decision fits the story Margo had been living.

The same questions arise in newer technologies: AI "griefbots" trained on a dead person's messages, and proposals to upload minds to computers. A griefbot may reproduce someone's style of speech, but is anything of the person there? Parfit's teletransporter, once a science fiction thought experiment, is a useful tool for thinking clearly about what we are actually getting.

vocabulary.definition: Being one and the same thing, as opposed to merely being exactly alike.
vocabulary.example: You at five and you today are numerically identical, though not qualitatively identical.

vocabulary.definition: Exact similarity in all properties, consistent with being two different things.
vocabulary.example: Two freshly printed copies of a book are qualitatively identical but numerically distinct.

vocabulary.definition: The question of what conditions make a person (or object) existing at one time the same as one existing at another.
vocabulary.example: Whether you would survive teleportation is a version of the persistence question.

vocabulary.definition: An overlapping chain of direct psychological connections, such as memories, intentions and character traits, linking a person over time.
vocabulary.example: Reid's general is psychologically continuous with the boy, though he has forgotten the flogging.

vocabulary.definition: The view that each of us is a human animal, whose persistence conditions are biological rather than psychological.
vocabulary.example: An animalist says you were once a fetus, though it had no memories or thoughts.

vocabulary.definition: A hypothetical case in which one person's psychology is divided so that two later people are each psychologically continuous with the original.
vocabulary.example: In fission, Lefty and Righty both remember your childhood, but they cannot both be you.

vocabulary.definition: Parfit's term for psychological connectedness and continuity, with any cause, which he argued is what matters in survival.
vocabulary.example: Parfit held that Relation R matters, even when it holds between one person and two later people.

vocabulary.definition: Parfit's view that a person's existence consists in the existence of a brain and body and a series of interrelated physical and mental events, with no further fact.
vocabulary.example: For a reductionist, there may be no answer to whether you survive fission, and nothing more to know.

thinkingExercise.title: Would You Step into the Teleporter?
thinkingExercise.prompt: Use the thought experiments to discover what you think matters about your own survival.
steps: Imagine being offered a free trip to Mars by teletransportation. Write down honestly whether you would go, and why.
Now imagine the Branch Line case happens to you. Does your answer to the first question change? If so, explain what the difference is.
Consider fission. Would you regard it as death, survival, or something in between? Rank fission against ordinary death and ordinary survival.
Decide which theory best fits your answers: psychological continuity, animalism, or Parfit's view that identity is not what matters.
Apply your theory to the Margo case: whose wishes should decide her treatment, and why?

summary: The persistence question concerns numerical identity over time despite qualitative change; the ship of Theseus shows that identity criteria such as continuity and sameness of parts can come apart.
Locke grounded personal identity in consciousness, often read as memory, and called 'person' a forensic term; Reid's brave officer (transitivity) and Butler's circularity objection challenged him.
Psychological continuity theories answer with overlapping chains and quasi-memory; animalism instead holds that we are human animals, citing the too many thinkers problem.
Teletransportation, the Branch Line case and fission show that psychological continuity can take a one-many form that identity cannot.
Parfit concluded that identity is not what matters; Relation R is, and personal identity is not a deep further fact. Critics cite framing effects (Williams) and narrative views (Schechtman).

quiz.question: Two identical new phones from the same factory are:
options: Numerically identical but qualitatively different
Qualitatively identical but numerically distinct
Both numerically and qualitatively identical
Neither
quiz.explanation: They share all their properties but are two different objects.

quiz.question: In Locke's prince and cobbler case, why does Locke say the cobbler's body now contains the prince?
options: Because it carries the prince's consciousness of his past life
Because the soul is a substance
Because the body has not changed
Because the prince is richer
quiz.explanation: For Locke, personal identity follows consciousness, not the body, so the person is the prince though the man is the cobbler.

quiz.question: Reid's brave officer objection shows that the simple memory criterion violates the transitivity of identity.
quiz.explanation: The general is the officer and the officer is the boy, but the general cannot remember the boy's flogging, so on the memory criterion he is not the boy.

quiz.question: How do psychological continuity theorists respond to Reid?
options: They abandon memory entirely
They accept that the general is not the boy
They define identity by overlapping chains of connections, which are transitive
They appeal to the soul
quiz.explanation: Like a rope made of overlapping fibers, continuity links the general to the boy through the officer.

quiz.question: What is animalism's 'too many thinkers' argument?
options: There are too many people on Earth
Each hemisphere is a thinker
Memory makes too many persons
If you are not the animal in your chair, there are two thinkers there, and you could not know which you are
quiz.explanation: Animalists say the simplest solution is that you are the thinking human animal.

quiz.question: In Parfit's Branch Line case, the original person survives on Earth, which suggests the replica on Mars is someone else.
quiz.explanation: Since the replica's relation to the original is the same as in ordinary teleportation, the case raises doubts about whether ordinary teleportation preserves identity.

quiz.question: Why can't you be both Lefty and Righty after fission?
options: Because one hemisphere always dominates
Because identity is one-one, and Lefty and Righty are two different people
Because brains cannot be divided
Because only Righty has memories
quiz.explanation: Lefty and Righty go on to lead different lives; one person cannot be two people.

quiz.question: Parfit argued that fission is about as bad as ordinary death.
quiz.explanation: Parfit argued fission is about as good as ordinary survival, since you get Relation R twice over, which shows identity is not what matters.

quiz.question: A family debates whether a content patient with dementia should be bound by a directive she wrote years ago. Which question from this lesson is most directly at stake?
options: Whether the patient's earlier and current selves are the same person, or connected enough for her past wishes to govern
Whether the ship of Theseus is the same ship
Whether the patient is qualitatively identical to her past self
Whether Hobbes was right about the planks
quiz.explanation: Dworkin and Dresser's debate turns on how personal identity and psychological connectedness relate the earlier and later self.

goDeeper.body:
Parfit's reductionism has a striking implication for rational self-interest. If what matters is Relation R, and R comes in degrees (you are strongly connected to yourself tomorrow and only weakly to yourself in fifty years), then perhaps it is rational to care less about your distant future. Parfit called this possibility a challenge to the **self-interest theory** of rationality, which says we should give equal weight to all parts of our own life. The self-interest theorist, Parfit argued, stands on unstable ground: either it should collapse toward caring equally about everyone (as identity becomes less important) or toward caring most about the present (as R weakens over time).

This connects to empirical work in psychology. Hal Hershfield and colleagues found, in brain-imaging studies, that thinking about one's future self engages patterns of brain activity more like those used to think about other people than those used to think about oneself now. People who feel more connected to their future selves tend to save more. Showing people age-progressed images of their own faces led them to allocate more to retirement savings in experiments. Whether this supports Parfit, or whether it shows a bias that rational self-interest should correct, is a matter of debate.

Another contemporary line comes from **four-dimensionalism**, defended by Theodore Sider and David Lewis (whose modal realism you may have met in the Logic track). On this view, objects, including persons, are extended in time as well as space, with temporal parts. In fission, there were two overlapping persons all along, sharing their early temporal parts, like two roads that share a stretch before diverging. This lets us say both Lefty and Righty were there from the start, preserving the importance of identity, though at the cost of an unusual metaphysics.

questions: If a perfect copy of you were created and you were destroyed, would anything important be lost?
Should someone be punished today for a crime they committed thirty years ago, if they have changed completely?
Is the self a story you tell, a living organism, or a chain of psychological connections?
